vignette: He sits across from me, fingers tracing the worn leather of his portfolio. At thirty, his face carries a tension that belongs to someone much older. I listen as he describes the crash, his voice steady but his hands restless. It is a Tuesday in November. The morning starts clear. He drives home from his office, a route he has taken for two years without a second thought. A delivery truck runs a red light at the intersection. The world tilts. Glass shaves the windshield. Airbags deploy like sudden storms. When he wakes in the back of the ambulance, the radio hums static, and his left hand shakes so hard he cannot clench it into a fist. The physical wounds heal quickly, but the roads never feel safe again. Within weeks, he stops driving. He tells me that the sound of a backfiring car still makes his chest tighten until he can barely draw breath. He begins taking the train, even though it adds an hour to his day. At the station, he always sits facing the tracks, knees locked, eyes fixed on the horizon. If a car slows nearby, his shoulders hunch forward, waiting for the impact that he knows is coming next. He is a third-generation Middle Eastern man who learned to keep his voice level during audits, but the silence now feels heavier than any argument. As a tax inspector, his life used to be built on ledgers, cross-referenced receipts, and the quiet certainty of numbers that add up exactly as they should. Now, the files on his desk feel like traps. He double-checks his calculations thirty times before submitting a report. He reads over audit notes until the ink blurs, certain he missed a decimal, certain the error will be found. His supervisor asks him to attend an in-person audit in the next city. He declines, citing a scheduling conflict. The truth sits heavier: he cannot look at highway maps on his phone without feeling the steering wheel slip through his palms. His divorce settled eight months before the collision, but he tells me now that the separation was only the first fracture. The accident widens the crack until everything falls through. He used to call his ex-wife's sister every Sunday. He stops. The phone sits on the counter, and when it rings, he lets it go to voicemail. He says the silence is easier. Some nights, he lies awake watching streetlights flicker through his blinds, replaying the moments before the impact. He wonders if he had glanced left instead of right, if he had tapped his brakes half a second sooner. The questions loop until dawn. When he does sleep, it comes in pieces. He wakes up gasping, heart hammering, convinced the tires are screeching outside his window. These days, he works in a corner office near the building's eastern wall. He prefers it because there are no windows overlooking the street. He eats lunch at his desk, reading tax codes aloud to steady his breathing. When a client's vehicle pulls up to drop off documents, he pauses, breath catching, until the engine fades. He has stopped going to the movies. He avoids highways, toll booths, even parking garages where the acoustics echo like tunnels. He tells me he feels detached from his own life, as if he is walking through a room full of people who speak a language he used to know. He laughs when someone jokes about road rage, but the laugh comes too quickly, too thin. He brings me a stack of completed audits every Friday, his handwriting precise, his margins exact. He leaves early on Thursdays because that is when the traffic patterns on the main avenue shift, and he cannot tolerate idle engines humming outside his window. He says he is learning to live with the quiet. He says he is learning to breathe through the static. I watch him fold his portfolio, tuck his keys into his coat pocket, and step out into the afternoon. The city moves around him, relentless and loud, while he walks a little farther from the curb, always looking over his shoulder, always waiting for the next light to turn red.
